intro: Formula 1 is the FIA's top single-seater championship: teams design and build their own cars within tight technical regulations and race them on circuits around the world. Every Grand Prix weekend combines practice, qualifying and a race, and points accumulate into two titles — the Drivers' and the Constructors' Championships. The FIA publishes the Sporting, Technical and Financial Regulations; 2026 marked a major reset with new power units and chassis rules.
inThirtySeconds: Qualifying decides the starting grid: the fastest lap starts on pole.
The top ten finishers score points, from 25 for the win down to 1 for tenth.
In a dry race, each car must use at least two different tyre compounds.
Flags, the safety car and stewards' penalties keep racing safe and fair.
objective: Score the most points across the season — for the driver and for the team.

facts.duration: Race of about 305 km (Monaco shorter), capped at 2 hours of running
equipment: Helmet, HANS device and fire-resistant overalls

scoring.label: Sprint
scoring.detail: At sprint weekends, a shorter race gives points to the top eight (8 down to 1).

scoring.label: Constructors
scoring.detail: A team's championship total is the sum of both drivers' points.

bodies.name: Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile
bodies.scope: Governing body; publishes the F1 regulations

bodies.name: Formula 1
bodies.scope: Commercial rights holder and championship organiser

rules.title: Knockout qualifying
rules.summary: Qualifying has three sessions — Q1, Q2 and Q3. The slowest cars are knocked out after Q1 and Q2; the top ten fight for pole in Q3.
rules.body: Grid positions follow the qualifying order, adjusted for any grid penalties. A driver who fails to set a time within 107% of the fastest Q1 time may need the stewards' permission to start.

rules.title: Sprint weekends
rules.summary: At selected events, a separate sprint qualifying and a short race of about 100 km take place before the main Grand Prix.
rules.body: The sprint awards points to the top eight. It does not set the grid for the main race, which has its own qualifying.

rules.title: Points and championships
rules.summary: The top ten in the race score 25, 18, 15, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and 1 points.
rules.body: There are two championships: drivers and constructors. If a race is stopped early and not resumed, reduced points may be awarded depending on how much distance was completed.

rules.title: Tyre rules
rules.summary: In a dry race, every driver must use at least two different dry-weather compounds, which forces at least one pit stop.
rules.body: Pirelli nominates three dry compounds per event (hard, medium, soft). If intermediate or wet tyres are used because of rain, the two-compound rule no longer applies.
rules.example: A driver starts on mediums and switches to hards: requirement met. Finishing on the starting compound without changing would bring a penalty.

rules.title: Pit stops and the pit lane
rules.summary: Cars must obey a speed limit in the pit lane; unsafe releases into the path of other cars are penalised.
rules.body: Crews can change all four tyres in a couple of seconds. Teams time stops tactically — an 'undercut' pits earlier to use fresh tyres to gain time.

rules.title: Safety car and red flags
rules.summary: After an incident, the safety car or virtual safety car slows the field; a red flag stops the session.
rules.body: Under the safety car, overtaking is forbidden and the field bunches up behind it. Under the virtual safety car, drivers must stay above a minimum time on each section. A red flag sends everyone to the pit lane.

rules.title: Flags
rules.summary: Yellow: danger, slow down, no overtaking. Blue: let a faster car lapping you through. Red: session stopped. Chequered: finish.
rules.body: A black-and-white diagonal flag is a warning for unsporting behaviour, and a black flag disqualifies a driver. Flags are complemented by marshal light panels and in-car displays.

rules.title: Stewards' penalties
rules.summary: Stewards can impose time penalties (5 or 10 seconds), drive-throughs, stop-and-go penalties, grid drops and penalty points.
rules.body: Common offences include causing a collision, leaving the track and gaining an advantage, exceeding track limits repeatedly, and speeding in the pit lane. Accumulating 12 penalty points on a superlicence within 12 months leads to a race ban.

rules.title: Component limits
rules.summary: Each driver has a limited number of power-unit components and gearbox parts per season; using more brings grid penalties.
rules.body: Cost-cap rules also limit team spending, and parc fermé conditions restrict changes to the car between qualifying and the race.

fouls.name: Track limits
fouls.description: Repeatedly leaving the track's white lines.
fouls.consequence: Lap time deleted, then time penalties

fouls.name: Causing a collision
fouls.description: Driver judged wholly or predominantly to blame.

fouls.name: Ignoring a red flag
fouls.description: Failing to slow and return to the pits.

flow.title: Qualifying
flow.description: Three knockout sessions decide the grid.

flow.title: Formation lap
flow.description: Cars warm their tyres and line up on the grid.

flow.title: Lights out
flow.description: Five red lights go out and the race begins.

positions.name: Driver
positions.role: Races the car and feeds back to engineers.

positions.name: Race engineer
positions.role: The driver's voice on the radio, managing strategy and car settings.

positions.name: Strategist
positions.role: Plans pit stops and tyre choices.

positions.name: Pit crew
positions.role: Changes tyres and makes repairs in seconds.

field.name: Circuit
field.surface: Asphalt with kerbs and run-off areas
notes: Pit lane with a speed limit
DRS or other overtaking aids depend on the current regulations

glossary.definition: First place on the starting grid.
Pitting earlier than a rival to gain time on fresh tyres.
Conditions limiting changes to the car after qualifying.

funFacts: The first Formula 1 World Championship race was held at Silverstone on 13 May 1950.
A modern pit stop can take less than two seconds.
